bull_bear.body:
- Brand consistency across units enforced through strong brand guidelines communicated to staff in all Units, with intellectual property rights registered and regular intellectual property audits carried out
- Internal controls in place to handle guest destruction and ensure travellers' safety during their stay
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Business slowdown / inadequate growth — Management explicitly flags that the risk of business slowdown, inadequate growth and negative returns has increased, calling hospitality 'the most affected' industry; its readiness plan (next-generation talent models, data-driven decision making, customer loyalty, operational flexibility) is still, in its own words, awaiting 'the path from theory to action'.
- Cyber security and guest data privacy — A security breach would require notifying past and present guests, is costly, damages the brand, and can expose the Company to liability claims for failure to protect data — a risk rising as more hospitality systems are digitised.
- Guest behaviour and premises liability — Guests are described as potentially the biggest direct and indirect threat to profitability; lawsuits from injured persons and damage to guestrooms are a stated risk to the bottom line, mitigated only through internal controls and closer management of property.
- Brand protection and consistency across dispersed units — Maintaining high and consistent standards is described as challenging due to the geographical distance separating each establishment; any infringement by an inferior brand may affect customers' perception, requiring registered IP rights and regular IP audits.
- Cost inflation in manpower, energy and food — Cost pressures related to manpower, energy and food inflation remained key considerations for operators during the year, and rising operational costs are named a continuing challenge — direct margin exposure for a single-segment hotel and F&B business.
- Macroeconomic, geopolitical and currency volatility affecting travel demand — Inflationary pressures across major economies, geopolitical uncertainties and currency volatility — particularly a relatively strong US dollar — continued to impact international travel demand and inbound tourism flows in select markets.
- Constrained airline capacity in Asia-Pacific — Regional airline capacity remained approximately 8%-12% below pre-pandemic (2019) levels during FY 2025-26, capping international travel volumes until fleet expansion and route additions narrow the gap.
- Rapidly changing guest expectations and technology adoption — Rapidly changing customer demands and a boom in guest-facing connected technologies are named as factors changing the sector's risk landscape; without digital and online-marketing capability management says it is increasingly difficult to build a profitable hotel business model.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.title: Competitive strengths

outlook.body:
- Focus on operational efficiency, cost optimization and strengthening domestic market presence to sustain growth
- Customer experience enhancement and strategic expansion aligned with India's long-term tourism-led growth trajectory
- Selective adoption of digital tools — evaluating together with employees which digital helpers offer real added value for guests and genuinely benefit the operation of the hotel units, alongside renewing IT structures and expanding digital communication channels
- Embedding a culture of proactive risk management by supporting acceptable and monitored risk-taking, balancing risk management against seizing emerging opportunities
- Protecting the brand by maintaining high and consistent standards across all units through strong brand guidelines communicated to staff, with registered IP rights and regular intellectual property audits
- Building downturn readiness through four steps: next-generation talent models, data-driven decision making, customer loyalty, and operational flexibility and responsiveness
- Conserving cash and ensuring liquidity for operations in the coming years (no dividend proposed for FY2025-26)
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: The annual report discloses no narrative expansion or capacity-addition programme. The only expansion-related item is a land purchase: the capital-commitments disclosure records advances paid towards the purchase of a plot, with a balance capital commitment still outstanding against that purchase as at 31 March 2026. Other estimated capital commitments not provided for were Nil at the year end.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Domestic tourism remained the key growth driver, supported by regional tourism, spiritual tourism, wellness retreats, staycations and short-duration leisure travel
- Indian hotel industry estimated to have recorded revenue growth of 10%-12% during FY 2025-26 on healthy demand, improved occupancy and firm pricing
- Robust domestic leisure demand from a growing middle class with rising disposable incomes; weddings, social events and spiritual tourism as key contributors
- MICE segment gaining traction, supported by government initiatives such as 'Meet in India' and new convention centres in Mumbai, Delhi and Jaipur
- Strengthening trend towards digital and online hotel bookings on higher smartphone penetration, better digital payment infrastructure and growing use of OTA platforms and mobile apps
- Rising demand for premium experiences, wellness-focused travel, sustainable tourism and blended 'bleisure' travel expected to keep shaping sector growth and operating strategies
- Improving air and road connectivity — domestic air passenger traffic estimated to have grown 8%-10% in FY 2025-26 — plus Swadesh Darshan 2.0 and PRASHAD tourism circuits improving access to emerging destinations
- Sector benefits from 100% FDI under the automatic route and government incentives promoting tourism infrastructure and hotel development
- Cost pressures related to manpower, energy and food inflation remained key considerations for operators; inflationary pressures and rising operational costs remain key challenges
- Growth in Tier-II and Tier-III cities and increasing preference for branded hospitality as structural demand drivers
- Rising cost of capital globally prompting a shift toward asset-light models like management contracts

products.body: - **Hospitality:** Accommodation services, Food and beverage services

end_markets.title: End Markets (RHP)
end_markets.body:
- India domestic tourism and leisure travel
- Corporate / business travel and MICE
- Weddings and social events

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Domestic tourism remained the key growth driver, supported by regional tourism, spiritual tourism, wellness retreats, staycations and short-duration leisure travel
- Indian hotel industry estimated to have recorded revenue growth of 10%-12% during FY 2025-26 on healthy demand, improved occupancy and firm pricing
- Robust domestic leisure demand from a growing middle class with rising disposable incomes; weddings, social events and spiritual tourism as key contributors
- MICE segment gaining traction, supported by government initiatives such as 'Meet in India' and new convention centres in Mumbai, Delhi and Jaipur
- Strengthening trend towards digital and online hotel bookings on higher smartphone penetration, better digital payment infrastructure and growing use of OTA platforms and mobile apps
- Rising demand for premium experiences, wellness-focused travel, sustainable tourism and blended 'bleisure' travel expected to keep shaping sector growth and operating strategies
- Improving air and road connectivity — domestic air passenger traffic estimated to have grown 8%-10% in FY 2025-26 — plus Swadesh Darshan 2.0 and PRASHAD tourism circuits improving access to emerging destinations
- Sector benefits from 100% FDI under the automatic route and government incentives promoting tourism infrastructure and hotel development
- Cost pressures related to manpower, energy and food inflation remained key considerations for operators; inflationary pressures and rising operational costs remain key challenges
- Growth in Tier-II and Tier-III cities and increasing preference for branded hospitality as structural demand drivers
- Rising cost of capital globally prompting a shift toward asset-light models like management contracts

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Focus on operational efficiency, cost optimization and strengthening domestic market presence to sustain growth
- Customer experience enhancement and strategic expansion aligned with India's long-term tourism-led growth trajectory
- Selective adoption of digital tools — evaluating together with employees which digital helpers offer real added value for guests and genuinely benefit the operation of the hotel units, alongside renewing IT structures and expanding digital communication channels
- Embedding a culture of proactive risk management by supporting acceptable and monitored risk-taking, balancing risk management against seizing emerging opportunities
- Protecting the brand by maintaining high and consistent standards across all units through strong brand guidelines communicated to staff, with registered IP rights and regular intellectual property audits
- Building downturn readiness through four steps: next-generation talent models, data-driven decision making, customer loyalty, and operational flexibility and responsiveness
- Conserving cash and ensuring liquidity for operations in the coming years (no dividend proposed for FY2025-26)

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: The annual report discloses no narrative expansion or capacity-addition programme. The only expansion-related item is a land purchase: the capital-commitments disclosure records advances paid towards the purchase of a plot, with a balance capital commitment still outstanding against that purchase as at 31 March 2026. Other estimated capital commitments not provided for were Nil at the year end.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Brand consistency across units enforced through strong brand guidelines communicated to staff in all Units, with intellectual property rights registered and regular intellectual property audits carried out
- Internal controls in place to handle guest destruction and ensure travellers' safety during their stay

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Business slowdown / inadequate growth — Management explicitly flags that the risk of business slowdown, inadequate growth and negative returns has increased, calling hospitality 'the most affected' industry; its readiness plan (next-generation talent models, data-driven decision making, customer loyalty, operational flexibility) is still, in its own words, awaiting 'the path from theory to action'.
- Cyber security and guest data privacy — A security breach would require notifying past and present guests, is costly, damages the brand, and can expose the Company to liability claims for failure to protect data — a risk rising as more hospitality systems are digitised.
- Guest behaviour and premises liability — Guests are described as potentially the biggest direct and indirect threat to profitability; lawsuits from injured persons and damage to guestrooms are a stated risk to the bottom line, mitigated only through internal controls and closer management of property.
- Brand protection and consistency across dispersed units — Maintaining high and consistent standards is described as challenging due to the geographical distance separating each establishment; any infringement by an inferior brand may affect customers' perception, requiring registered IP rights and regular IP audits.
- Cost inflation in manpower, energy and food — Cost pressures related to manpower, energy and food inflation remained key considerations for operators during the year, and rising operational costs are named a continuing challenge — direct margin exposure for a single-segment hotel and F&B business.
- Macroeconomic, geopolitical and currency volatility affecting travel demand — Inflationary pressures across major economies, geopolitical uncertainties and currency volatility — particularly a relatively strong US dollar — continued to impact international travel demand and inbound tourism flows in select markets.
- Constrained airline capacity in Asia-Pacific — Regional airline capacity remained approximately 8%-12% below pre-pandemic (2019) levels during FY 2025-26, capping international travel volumes until fleet expansion and route additions narrow the gap.
- Rapidly changing guest expectations and technology adoption — Rapidly changing customer demands and a boom in guest-facing connected technologies are named as factors changing the sector's risk landscape; without digital and online-marketing capability management says it is increasingly difficult to build a profitable hotel business model.
